extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general literate public interested in manners, moral essays, and light satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars relevant to composing short moral/society essays and satirical observations in the Spectator tradition — balancing entertainment, moral instruction, character sketches, and vivid anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeless representation in portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Masters in Painting never care for drawing People in the Fashion; as very well knowing that the Headdress, or Periwig, that now prevails, and gives a Grace to their Portraitures at present, will make a very odd Figure, and perhaps look monstrous in the Eyes of Posterity. For this Reason they often represent an illustrious Person in a Roman Habit, or in some other Dress that never varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer elements that are not tied to fleeting fashions when you wish a work to endure; choose 'everlasting drapery' or timeless attributes so the subject will not appear ridiculous to future readers/viewers. (Applied metaphorically to writing: avoid ephemeral localities of mode when aiming for lasting effect.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on outward appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: This was a childish Amusement when I was carried away with outward Appearance, but you make a deeper Impression, and affect the secret Springs of the Mind;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial detail and mere fashion-change are lesser arts; stronger prose moves readers by addressing deeper sentiments and character rather than relying only on external, fashionable trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Variety of your Subjects surprizes me as much as a Box of Pictures did formerly, in which there was only one Face ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wide range of topics keeps the reader engaged; shifting subjects provide fresh amusements and allow the writer to surprise and instruct across many small pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affect the secret springs of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: you make a deeper Impression, and affect the secret Springs of the Mind; you charm the Fancy, sooth the Passions, and insensibly lead the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper that you so well describe;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to move readers subtly: charm imagination, calm passions, and gently shape temper and sentiment rather than using heavy-handed didacticism. Emotional and moral influence should be gradual and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine entertainment with improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: I constantly peruse your Paper ... and really it gives a grateful Relish ... each Paragraph is freight either with useful or delightful Notions, and I never fail of being highly diverted or improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful essays both amuse ('delightful Notions') and instruct ('useful Notions'). Strive for pieces that entertain while imparting moral or practical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, observable detail for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most fashionable Women I met with ... Her Commode was not half a Foot high, and her Petticoat within some Yards of a modish Circumference ... I observed a young Fellow with a tolerable Periwig, had it not been covered with a Hat that was shaped in the Ramillie Cock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic description benefits from precise, tangible particulars (odd proportions, specific costume elements, small local curiosities). Such details both authenticate the scene and provide material for gentle ridicule or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray complementary virtues in character sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: How different are the Lives of Aristus and Aspasia? the innocent Vivacity of the one is tempered and composed by the chearful Gravity of the other. The Wife grows wise by the Discourses of the Husband, and the Husband good-humour'd by the Conversations of the Wife. Their Virtues are blended in their Children, and diffuse through the whole Family a perpetual Spirit of Benevolence, Complacency, and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character portrayals are effective when they show balance and mutual influence: contrasting but complementary traits produce believable, socially instructive figures whose interactions model desirable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke emotional complexity (mixture of terror and sorrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a sort of Delight, which is alternately mixed with Terror and Sorrow, in the Contemplation of Death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To move readers profoundly, allow for mixed emotions — e.g., awe together with grief. Presenting noble responses to extreme situations (heroic resignation, composed death) intensifies admiration and moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary stories to inspire moral reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: We are affected with these respective Manners of Behaviour, as we secretly believe the Part of the Dying Person imitable by our selves ... When Phocion's good Actions had met with the like Reward ... how gracefully does he support his Illustrious Character to the very last Instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including historical or exemplary anecdotes of noble behavior provides models for readers to admire and emulate; such exempla add moral weight and elevate the essay's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding: modesty and concealment of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no ordinary Part of humane Life which expresseth so much a good Mind ... Such a Man, when he falleth in the way with Persons of Simplicity and Innocence, however knowing he may be in the Ways of Men, will not vaunt himself thereof; but will the rather hide his Superiority to them, that he may not be painful unto them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social conduct presented as exemplary emphasizes humility: a well-bred person conceals superiority and acts to avoid mortifying simpler companions. Essays that praise such conduct model civility and restraint.
